subChunks.title: Render Props and Higher-Order Components
subChunks.hookHtml: Before hooks, render props and higher-order components (HOCs) were the primary patterns for reusing stateful logic across components. Custom hooks largely replaced them — but render props and HOCs still appear in production codebases, third-party libraries, and interview questions. Understanding them makes you fluent in the full history of React patterns and capable of working with any legacy codebase.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Render Prop pattern

A render prop is a prop whose value is a function that returns JSX. The component calls this function to render its content, sharing its internal state with the caller:

// A DataFetcher that exposes its state via a render prop:
function DataFetcher({ url, render }) {
  const [data, setData] = useState(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch(url)
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(setData)
      .catch(setError)
      .finally(() => setLoading(false));
  }, [url]);

  return render({ data, loading, error });
}

// Usage — the caller controls how to display the data:
<DataFetcher
  url="/api/quests"
  render={({ data, loading, error }) => {
    if (loading) return <p>Loading...</p>;
    if (error) return <p>Error: {error.message}</p>;
    return <QuestList quests={data} />;
  }}
/>

The children prop can also be a function — this is called the "children as a function" pattern:

<DataFetcher url="/api/quests">
  {({ data, loading }) => loading ? <Spinner /> : <QuestList quests={data} />}
</DataFetcher>

Higher-Order Components (HOCs)

A HOC is a function that takes a component and returns a new component with enhanced behaviour:

// HOC that adds authentication gating:
function withAuth(WrappedComponent) {
  return function AuthenticatedComponent(props) {
    const { user } = useAuth();

    if (!user) {
      return <Navigate to="/login" />;
    }

    return <WrappedComponent {...props} user={user} />;
  };
}

// HOC that adds loading state:
function withLoading(WrappedComponent) {
  return function WithLoadingComponent({ isLoading, ...props }) {
    if (isLoading) return <Spinner />;
    return <WrappedComponent {...props} />;
  };
}

// Usage:
const AuthenticatedDashboard = withAuth(Dashboard);
const LoadingAwareList = withLoading(QuestList);

HOC conventions

// 1. Always forward the display name for DevTools:
AuthenticatedComponent.displayName = `withAuth(${WrappedComponent.displayName || WrappedComponent.name})`;

// 2. Pass all props through to the wrapped component:
return <WrappedComponent {...props} />;

// 3. Never mutate the original component — always wrap:
// ❌ WrappedComponent.prototype.componentDidMount = ...
// ✅ Return a new component that wraps WrappedComponent

Render props vs HOCs vs Hooks

Vex: "Custom hooks replaced render props and HOCs for most new code. But you'll encounter them in legacy codebases and third-party libraries — React Router's withRouter, Redux's connect, Relay's createFragmentContainer. Knowing the pattern means you can read and extend existing code confidently. When writing new code: prefer custom hooks. When wrapping third-party components or building cross-cutting concerns: HOCs are still valid."

// The same logic — three implementations:

// 1. Render prop:
<Mouse render={({ x, y }) => <Cursor x={x} y={y} />} />

// 2. HOC:
const TrackedCursor = withMousePosition(Cursor);

// 3. Custom hook (modern, preferred):
function Cursor() {
  const { x, y } = useMousePosition();
  return <div style={{ left: x, top: y }} />;
}

storyBeats.text: Vex opens an ancient tome — code written before hooks existed. Every pattern for sharing logic involved either render props or higher-order components. 'You don't need to write these often,' she says, 'but you need to read them fluently.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Render props share state by calling a function prop with that state as arguments. HOCs wrap a component with new behaviour. Custom hooks made both largely redundant for new code — but half the libraries you'll use were written with these patterns. Know them.

storyBeats.speaker: Render prop vs equivalent custom hook

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Implement both patterns:

  • Build a <Toggle render /> render prop component that manages an on boolean state and passes { on, toggle } to the render function. Use it to build a show/hide password toggle.
  • Build a withBadge(WrappedComponent, badgeText) HOC that renders the wrapped component with a badge overlay in the top-right corner. Forward all props. Set a proper displayName.

guidedPracticeTests.label: Password input renders as password type by default
Toggle shows the input as text after click

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a withErrorBoundary(WrappedComponent, fallback) HOC that wraps the component in an ErrorBoundary. The HOC should accept an optional fallback render function. Then build an equivalent custom hook approach for any recoverable logic, and write a paragraph in comments comparing the two approaches — when would you use the HOC vs a hooks-based solution?
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain render props and higher-order components as patterns for sharing stateful logic. For each: what problem does it solve, how does it work, and what is its main limitation? Then explain why custom hooks largely replaced them — what does a hook give you that the older patterns don't?

options: A prop whose value is a function that returns JSX — the component calls this function and passes its internal state as arguments
A prop that controls whether a component re-renders
A prop that replaces the component's default render method
Any prop whose name starts with 'render'
questions.answer: A prop whose value is a function that returns JSX — the component calls this function and passes its internal state as arguments
questions.explanation: A render prop is a function-valued prop that the component calls to render output, passing its state as arguments. This lets the caller control presentation while the component manages the logic. The name 'render' is conventional — 'children' as a function is also common.

options: A function that takes a component and returns a new enhanced component
A component that renders above other components in the tree
A component with more than 100 lines of code
A component that uses React.memo for optimisation
questions.answer: A function that takes a component and returns a new enhanced component
questions.explanation: A HOC is a pure function: it takes a component as input and returns a new component that wraps it with additional behaviour (authentication, logging, loading state, etc.). It doesn't modify the input component — it wraps it. The pattern mirrors higher-order functions in functional programming.

questions.prompt: A HOC wraps a component but it appears as 'Component' in React DevTools instead of 'withAuth(Dashboard)'. What convention should you apply?
options: Export the HOC with a named export instead of default
Add a static name property to the wrapped component
questions.explanation: React DevTools uses the displayName property to label components. HOCs return anonymous function components by default — DevTools shows 'Component' or the inner function name. Setting displayName to 'withAuth(Dashboard)' makes the component tree readable. This is a convention all well-written HOC libraries follow.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer a HOC over a custom hook for sharing logic in new code?
options: When you need to wrap a third-party component you can't modify, or enforce a cross-cutting concern (auth gate, error boundary) at the component level
Always — HOCs are more composable than custom hooks
When the logic involves state — hooks can't manage state effectively
When you need to avoid re-renders — HOCs are faster than hooks
questions.answer: When you need to wrap a third-party component you can't modify, or enforce a cross-cutting concern (auth gate, error boundary) at the component level
questions.explanation: Custom hooks are preferred for new logic sharing because they're simpler, compose cleanly, and don't add extra component tree nodes. HOCs remain valid when: wrapping third-party components (you can't add a hook inside them), implementing class component patterns, or when the enhancement must work at the component level regardless of the component's internals (auth gating, error boundaries).
